title: Can AI design an optimal retrieval schedule?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton describes how he used Claude, with no technical background, to add an optimal spacing algorithm to his free Ultimate Retrieval Tool for maths teachers. Previously teachers had to choose which skills went into a Do Now or Low-Stakes Quiz and devise their own schedule for revisiting them. Now teachers list the skills taught to a class, and the tool selects what to retrieve and when. A simple green, amber or red rating of how the class performed lets skills that students know well be revisited after longer gaps while struggling skills return sooner. Teachers need only a class code, with no login, so the system remembers topics, results and retrieval counts across devices. He ties the tool to his view that homework should become preparation for an in-class assessment, and he treats the project as an example of teachers being well placed to direct AI because they explain things well.
points: The tool now picks which of 700-plus maths skills to retrieve, removing the burden of tracking every topic and building a spacing algorithm by hand.
A green, amber or red tick after reviewing a quiz lets longer gaps follow strong performance and quicker revisits follow weak performance.
Class codes replace logins, so the system remembers taught topics, results and retrieval counts on any device.
The one-click follow-up quiz supports a model in which homework is preparation for a paper-based in-class check rather than an assessment itself.
The account shows that teachers with no coding skills can build useful classroom tools by explaining clearly to AI what they want.
quotes: I’ve built an optimal spacing schedule algorithm into my free Ultimate Retrieval Tool, so your students always get the right Do Now or Low-Stakes Quiz when they need it.
Even if they did, teachers still had to figure out their own algorithm for when to revisit those skills and how often, to flatten the forgetting curve.
Skills where students perform well can have longer gaps before their next exposure, whereas skills where students struggle need revisiting sooner.
When teachers review answers to a Do Now or Low-Stakes Quiz, they simply tick green, amber, or red to indicate the rough proportion of students who got the question correct.
I think this is the only way to make homework work in the AI world: to repurpose it so it’s preparation for an in-class assessment, as opposed to being an assessment itself.

As long as you can explain to AI what you want to build - and as I argued in that piece, teachers are uniquely qualified to do so because they are good at explaining and have infinite levels of patience - then AI can do the building for you.

Without regular retrieval opportunities that are optimised in terms of content and timing, teachers and their students will find themselves in that demoralising cycle: they understand something at the time, but later at the very moment they need to recall it (often a high-stakes exam), it’s gone.
